entries.f1edcf936b9cb6e5bff5a6b20088b3d5fbcae499: <div sID="gen11864" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="77" osisID="Ps.77" sID="Ps.77"/> <div eID="gen11864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11865" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11866" type="x-p"/> This psalm, according to the method of many other psalms, begins with sorrowful complaints but ends with comfortable encouragements. The complaints seem to be of personal grievances, but the encouragements relate to the public concerns of the church, so that it is not certain whether it was penned upon a personal or a public account. If they were private troubles that he was groaning under, it teaches us that what God has wrought for his church in general may be improved for the comfort of particular believers; if it was some public calamity that he is here lamenting, his speaking of it so feelingly, as if it had been some particular trouble of his own, shows how much we should lay to heart the interests of the church of God and make them ours. One of the rabbin says, This psalm is spoken in the dialect of the captives; and therefore some think it was penned in the captivity in Babylon. I. The psalmist complains here of the deep impressions which his troubles made upon his spirits, and the temptation he was in to despair of relief, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.1-Ps.77.10">ver. 1-10</reference>. II. He encourages himself to hope that it would be well at last, by the remembrance of God's former appearances for the help of his people, of which he gives several instances, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.11-Ps.77.20">ver. 11-20</reference>. In singing this psalm we must take shame to ourselves for all our sinful distrusts of God, and of his providence and promise, and give to him the glory of his power and goodness by a thankful commemoration of what he has done for us formerly and a cheerful dependence on him for the future.
entries.8898152eee65ed2f1db8c387cce2de14077fc26f: <div eID="gen11866" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11865" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Prevailing Melancholy; Mournful Supplications.</title> <div sID="gen11867" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I cried unto God with my voice, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto God with my voice; and he gave ear unto me. <hi type="super">2</hi> In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord: my sore ran in the night, and ceased not: my soul refused to be comforted. <hi type="super">3</hi> I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah. <hi type="super">4</hi> Thou holdest mine eyes waking: I am so troubled that I cannot speak. <hi type="super">5</hi> I have considered the days of old, the years of ancient times. <hi type="super">6</hi> I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search. <hi type="super">7</hi> Will the Lord cast off for ever? and will he be favourable no more? <hi type="super">8</hi> Is his mercy clean gone for ever? doth <hi type="italic">his</hi> promise fail for evermore? <hi type="super">9</hi> Hath God forgotten to be gracious? hath he in anger shut up his tender mercies? Selah. <hi type="super">10</hi> And I said, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> my infirmity: <hi type="italic">but I will remember</hi> the years of the right hand of the most High. <div eID="gen11867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11868" type="x-p"/> We have here the lively portraiture of a good man under prevailing melancholy, fallen into and sinking in that horrible pit and that miry clay, but struggling to get out. Drooping saints, that are of a sorrowful spirit, may here as in a glass see their own faces. The conflict which the psalmist had with his griefs and fears seems to have been over when he penned this record of it; for he says (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">I cried unto God, and he gave ear unto me,</hi> which, while the struggle lasted, he had not the comfortable sense of, as he had afterwards; but he inserts it in the beginning of his narrative as an intimation that his trouble did not end in despair; for God heard him, and, at length, he knew that he heard him. Observe, <div eID="gen11868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11869" type="x-p"/> I. His melancholy prayers. Being afflicted, he prayed (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.13">Jam. v. 13</reference>), and, being in an agony, he prayed more earnestly (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">My voice was unto God, and I cried, even with my voice unto God.</hi> He was full of complaints, loud complaints, but he directed them to God, and turned them all into prayers, vocal prayers, very earnest and importunate. Thus he gave vent to his grief and gained some ease; and thus he took the right way in order to relief (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">In the day of my trouble I sought the Lord.</hi> Note, Days of trouble must be days of prayer, days of inward trouble especially, when God seems to have withdrawn from us; we must seek him and seek till we find him. In the day of his trouble he did not seek for the diversion of business or recreation, to shake off his trouble that way, but he sought God, and his favour and grace. Those that are under trouble of mind must not think to drink it away, or laugh it away, but must pray it away. <hi type="italic">My hand was stretched out in the night and ceased not;</hi> so Dr. Hammond reads the following words, as speaking the incessant importunity of his prayers. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.143.5-Ps.143.6">Ps. cxliii. 5, 6</reference>. <div eID="gen11869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11870" type="x-p"/> II. His melancholy grief. Grief may then be called melancholy indeed, 1. When it admits of no intermission; such was his: <hi type="italic">My sore,</hi> or wound, <hi type="italic">ran in the night,</hi> and bled inwardly, and it ceased not, no, not in the time appointed for rest and sleep. 2. When it admits of no consolation; and that also as his case: <hi type="italic">My soul refused to be comforted;</hi> he had no mind to hearken to those that would be his comforters. <hi type="italic">As vinegar upon nitre, so is he that sings songs to a heavy heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.20">Prov. xxv. 20</reference>. Nor had he any mind to think of those things that would be his comforts; he put them far from him, as one that indulged himself in sorrow. Those that are in sorrow, upon any account, do not only prejudice themselves, but affront God, if they refuse to be comforted. <div eID="gen11870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11871" type="x-p"/> III. His melancholy musings. He pored so much upon the trouble, whatever it was, personal or public, that, 1. The methods that should have relieved him did but increase his grief, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.3">v. 3</reference>. (1.) One would have thought that the remembrance of God would comfort him, but it did not: <hi type="italic">I remembered God and was troubled,</hi> as poor Job (<reference osisRef="Job.23.15">ch. xxiii. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">I am troubled at his presence; when I consider I am afraid of him.</hi> When he remembered God his thoughts fastened only upon his justice, and wrath, and dreadful majesty, and thus God himself became a terror to him. (2.) One would have thought that pouring out his soul before God would give him ease, but it did not; he <hi type="italic">complained, and</hi> yet his <hi type="italic">spirit was overwhelmed,</hi> and sank under the load. 2. The means of his present relief were denied him, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">v. 4</reference>. He could not enjoy sleep, which, if it be quiet and refreshing, is a parenthesis to our griefs and cares: "<hi type="italic">Thou holdest my eyes waking</hi> with thy terrors, which make me full of <hi type="italic">tossings to and fro until the dawning of the day.</hi>" He could not speak, by reason of the disorder of his thoughts, the tumult of his spirits, and the confusion his mind was in: He <hi type="italic">kept silence even from good</hi> while <hi type="italic">his heart was hot within him;</hi> he was <hi type="italic">ready to burst like a new bottle</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.32.19">Job xxxii. 19</reference>), and yet so troubled that he could not speak and refresh himself. Grief never preys so much upon the spirits as when it is thus smothered and pent up. <div eID="gen11871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11872" type="x-p"/> IV. His melancholy reflections (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.5-Ps.77.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I have considered the days of old,</hi> and compared them with the present days; and our former prosperity does but aggravate our present calamities: for we see not the wonders that our fathers told us off." Melancholy people are apt to pore altogether upon the days of old and the years of ancient times, and to magnify them, for the justifying of their own uneasiness and discontent at the present posture of affairs. But <hi type="italic">say not thou</hi> that <hi type="italic">the former days were better than these,</hi> because it is more than thou knowest whether they were or no, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.10">Eccl. vii. 10</reference>. Neither let the remembrance of the comforts we have lost make us unthankful for those that are left, or impatient under our crosses. Particularly, he <hi type="italic">called to remembrance his song in the night,</hi> the comforts with which he had supported himself in his former sorrows and entertained himself in his former solitude. These songs he remembered, and tried if he could not sing them over again; but he was out of tune for them, and the remembrance of them did but <hi type="italic">pour out his soul in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Ps. xliii. 4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job xxxv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen11872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11873" type="x-p"/> V. His melancholy fears and apprehensions: "<hi type="italic">I communed with my own heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.77.6">v. 6</reference>. Come, my soul, what will be the issue of these things? What can I think of them and what can I expect they will come to at last? I <hi type="italic">made diligent search</hi> into the causes of my trouble, enquiring wherefore God contended with me and what would be the consequences of it. And thus I began to reason, <hi type="italic">Will the Lord cast off for ever,</hi> as he does for the present? He is not now favourable; and <hi type="italic">will he be favourable no more? His mercy</hi> is now gone; <hi type="italic">and is it clean gone for ever? His promise</hi> now fails; and <hi type="italic">does it fail for evermore?</hi> God is not now gracious; but <hi type="italic">has he forgotten to be gracious?</hi> His <hi type="italic">tender mercies</hi> have been withheld, perhaps in wisdom; but <hi type="italic">are they shut up,</hi> shut up <hi type="italic">in anger?</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.77.7-Ps.77.9">v. 7-9</reference>. This is the language of a disconsolate deserted soul, walking in darkness and having no light, a case not uncommon even with those that <hi type="italic">fear the Lord and obey the voice of his servant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Isa. l. 10</reference>. He may here be looked upon, 1. As groaning under a sore trouble. God hid his face from him, and withdrew the usual tokens of his favour. Note, Spiritual trouble is of all trouble most grievous to a gracious soul; nothing wounds and pierces it like the apprehensions of God's being angry, the suspending of his favour and the superseding of his promise; this wounds the spirit; and who can bear that? 2. As grappling with a strong temptation. Note, God's own people, in a cloudy and dark day, may be tempted to make desperate conclusions about their own spiritual state and the condition of God's church and kingdom in the world, and, as to both, to give up all for gone. We may be tempted to think that God has abandoned us and cast us off, that the covenant of grace fails us, and that the tender mercy of our God shall be for ever withheld from us. But we must not give way to such suggestions as these. If fear and melancholy ask such peevish questions, let faith answer them from the Scripture: <hi type="italic">Will the Lord cast off for ever?</hi> God forbid, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom. xi. 1</reference>. No; <hi type="italic">the Lord will not cast off his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.14">Ps. xciv. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Will he be favourable no more?</hi> Yes, he will; <hi type="italic">for, though he cause grief, yet will he have compassion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.3.32">Lam. iii. 32</reference>. <hi type="italic">Is his mercy clean gone for ever?</hi> No; his <hi type="italic">mercy endures for ever;</hi> as it is <hi type="italic">from everlasting,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">to everlasting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.103.17">Ps. ciii. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">Doth his promise fail for evermore?</hi> No; <hi type="italic">it is impossible for God to lie,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.6.18">Heb. vi. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Hath God forgotten to be gracious?</hi> No; <hi type="italic">he cannot deny himself,</hi> and his own name which he hath proclaimed <hi type="italic">gracious and merciful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.34.6">Exod. xxxiv. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Has he in anger shut up his tender mercies?</hi> No; they are <hi type="italic">new every morning</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.23">Lam. iii. 23</reference>); and therefore, <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up, Ephraim?</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8-Hos.11.9">Hos. xi. 8, 9</reference>. Thus was he going on with his dark and dismal apprehensions when, on a sudden, he first checked himself with that word, <hi type="italic">Selah,</hi> "Stop there; go no further; let us hear no more of these unbelieving surmises;" and he then chid himself (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I said, This is my infirmity.</hi> He is soon aware that it is not well said, and therefore, "<hi type="italic">Why art thou cast down, O my soul? I said, This is my affliction</hi>" (so some understand it); "This is the calamity that falls to my lot and I must make the best of it; every one has his affliction, his trouble in the flesh; and this is mine, the cross I must take up." Or, rather, "This is my sin; it is my iniquity, the plague of my own heart." These doubts and fears proceed from the want and weakness of faith and the corruption of a distempered mind. note, (1.) We all know that concerning ourselves of which we must say, "<hi type="italic">This is our infirmity,</hi> a sin that most easily besets us." (2.) Despondency of spirit, and distrust of God, under affliction, are too often the infirmities of good people, and, as such, are to be reflected upon by us with sorrow and shame, as by the psalmist here: <hi type="italic">This is my infirmity.</hi> When at any time it is working in us we must thus suppress the rising of it, and not suffer the evil spirit to speak. We must argue down the insurrections of unbelief, as the psalmist here: <hi type="italic">But I will remember the years of the right hand of the Most High.</hi> He had been considering the <hi type="italic">years of ancient times</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.5">v. 5</reference>), the blessings formerly enjoyed, the remembrance of which did only add to his grief; but now he considered them as <hi type="italic">the years of the right hand of the Most High,</hi> that those blessings of ancient times came from the Ancient of days, from the power and sovereign disposal of his right hand who is <hi type="italic">over all, God, blessed for ever,</hi> and this satisfied him; for may not the Most High with his right hand make what changes he pleases?
entries.0954e94477ed32b2d979abceca90ff5b910bc1f3: <div eID="gen11873" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Acknowledgments of the Divine Majesty, of God's Wonders Wrought for Israel.</title> <div sID="gen11874" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> I will remember the works of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : surely I will remember thy wonders of old. 12 I will meditate also of all thy work, and talk of thy doings. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thy way, O God, <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the sanctuary: who <hi type="italic">is so</hi> great a God as <hi type="italic">our</hi> God? <hi type="super">14</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> the God that doest wonders: thou hast declared thy strength among the people. <hi type="super">15</hi> Thou hast with <hi type="italic">thine</hi> arm redeemed thy people, the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah. 16 The waters saw thee, O God, the waters saw thee; they were afraid: the depths also were troubled. <hi type="super">17</hi> The clouds poured out water: the skies sent out a sound: thine arrows also went abroad. <hi type="super">18</hi> The voice of thy thunder <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the heaven: the lightnings lightened the world: the earth trembled and shook. <hi type="super">19</hi> Thy way <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the sea, and thy path in the great waters, and thy footsteps are not known. <hi type="super">20</hi> Thou leddest thy people like a flock by the hand of Moses and Aaron. <div eID="gen11874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11875" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here recovers himself out of the great distress and plague he was in, and silences his own fears of God's casting off his people by the remembrance of the great things he had done for them formerly, which though he had in vain tried to quiet himself with (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.5-Ps.77.6">v. 5, 6</reference>) yet he tried again, and, upon this second trial, found it not in vain. It is good to persevere in the proper means for the strengthening of faith, though they do not prove effectual at first: "<hi type="italic">I will remember, surely I will,</hi> what God has done for his people of old, till I can thence infer a happy issue of the present dark dispensation," <reference osisRef="Ps.77.11-Ps.77.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. Note, 1. The works of the Lord, for his people, have been wondrous works. 2. They are recorded for us, that they may be remembered by us. 3. That we may have benefit by the remembrance of them we must meditate upon them, and dwell upon them in our thoughts, and must talk of them, that we may inform ourselves and others further concerning them. 4. The due remembrance of the works of God will be a powerful antidote against distrust of his promise and goodness; for he is God and changes not. If he begin, he will finish his work and bring forth the top-stone. <div eID="gen11875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11876" type="x-p"/> Two things, in general, satisfied him very much: <div eID="gen11876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11877" type="x-p"/> I. That <hi type="italic">God's way is in the sanctuary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.77.13">v. 13</reference>. It is <hi type="italic">in holiness,</hi> so some. When we cannot solve the particular difficulties that may arise in our constructions of the divine providence, this we are sure of, in general, that God is holy in all his works, that they are all worthy of himself and consonant to the eternal purity and rectitude of his nature. He has holy ends in all he does, and will be sanctified in every dispensation of his providence. His way is according to his promise, which he has spoken in his holiness and made known in the sanctuary. What he has done is according to what he has said and may be interpreted by it; and from what he has said we may easily gather that he will not cast off his people for ever. God's way is for the sanctuary, and for the benefit of it. All he does is intended for the good of his church. <div eID="gen11877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11878" type="x-p"/> II. That God's <hi type="italic">way is in the sea.</hi> Though God is holy, just, and good, in all he does, yet we cannot give an account of the reasons of his proceedings, nor make any certain judgment of his designs: <hi type="italic">His path is in the great waters and his footsteps are not known,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">v. 19</reference>. God's ways are like the deep waters which cannot be fathomed (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Ps. xxxvi. 6</reference>), like the way of a ship in the sea, which cannot be tracked, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18-Prov.30.19">Prov. xxx. 18, 19</reference>. God's proceedings are always to be acquiesced in, but cannot always be accounted for. He specifies some particulars, for which he goes as far back as the infancy of the Jewish church, and from which he gathers, 1. That there is no God to be compared with the God of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is so great a God as our God?</hi> Let us first give to God the glory of the great things he has done for his people, and acknowledge him, therein, great above all comparison; and then we may take to ourselves the comfort of what he has done and encourage ourselves with it. 2. That he is a God of almighty power (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.14">v. 14</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Thou art the God that</hi> alone <hi type="italic">doest wonders,</hi> above the power of any creature; <hi type="italic">thou hast</hi> visibly, and beyond any contradiction, <hi type="italic">declared thy strength among the people.</hi>" What God has done for his church has been a standing declaration of his almighty power, for therein he has made bare his everlasting arm. (1.) God brought Israel out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.15">v. 15</reference>. This was the beginning of mercy to them, and was yearly to be commemorated among them in the passover: <hi type="italic">"Thou hast with thy arm,</hi> stretched out in so many miracles, <hi type="italic">redeemed thy people</hi> out of the hand of the Egyptians." Though they were delivered by power, yet they are said to be redeemed, as if it had been done by price, because it was typical of the great redemption, which was to be wrought out, in the fulness of time, both by price and power. Those that were redeemed are here called not only <hi type="italic">the sons of Jacob,</hi> to whom the promise was made, but <hi type="italic">of Joseph</hi> also, who had a most firm and lively belief of the performance of it; for, when he was dying, he made mention of the departing of the children of Israel out of Egypt, and gave commandment concerning his bones. (2.) He divided the Red Sea before them (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">The waters</hi> gave way, and a lane was made through that crowd instantly, as if they had seen God himself at the head of the armies of Israel, and had retired for fear of him. Not only the surface of the waters, but <hi type="italic">the depths, were troubled,</hi> and opened to the right and to the left, in obedience to his word of command. (3.) He destroyed the Egyptians (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">The clouds poured out water</hi> upon them, while the pillar of fire, like an umbrella over the camp of Israel, sheltered it from the shower, in which, as in the deluge, the waters that were above the firmament concurred with those that were beneath the firmament to destroy the rebels. Then <hi type="italic">the skies sent out a sound; thy arrows also went abroad,</hi> which is explained (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">The voice of thy thunder was heard in the heaven</hi> (that was the sound which the skies sent forth); <hi type="italic">the lightnings lightened the world</hi>—those were the arrows which went abroad, by which the host of the Egyptians was discomfited, with so much terror that <hi type="italic">the earth</hi> of the adjacent coast <hi type="italic">trembled and shook.</hi> Thus God's way was in the sea, for the destruction of his enemies, as well as for the salvation of his people; and yet when the waters returned to their place <hi type="italic">his footsteps were not known</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">v. 19</reference>); there was no mark set upon the place, as there was, afterwards, in Jordan, <reference osisRef="Josh.4.9">Josh. iv. 9</reference>. We do not read in the story of Israel's passing through the Red Sea that there were thunders and lightning, and an earthquake; yet there might be, and Josephus says there were, such displays of the divine terror upon that occasion. But it may refer to the thunders, lightnings, and earth quakes, that were at Mount Sinai when the law was given. (4.) He took his people Israel under his own guidance and protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.77.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou leddest thy people like a flock.</hi> They being weak and helpless, and apt to wander like a flock of sheep, and lying exposed to the beasts of prey, God went before them with all the care and tenderness of a shepherd, that they might not fail. The pillar of cloud and fire led them; yet that is not here taken notice of, but the agency of Moses and Aaron, by whose hand God led them; they could not do it without God, but God did it with and by them. Moses was their governor, Aaron their high priest; they were guides, overseers, and rulers to Israel, and by them God led them. The right and happy administration of the two great ordinances of magistracy and ministry is, though not so great a miracle, yet as great a mercy to any people as the pillar of cloud and fire was to Israel in the wilderness. <div eID="gen11878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11879" type="x-p"/> The psalm concludes abruptly, and does not apply those ancient instances of God's power to the present distresses of the church, as one might have expected. But as soon as the good man began to meditate on these things he found he had gained his point; his very entrance upon this matter <hi type="italic">gave him light</hi> and joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.130">Ps. cxix. 130</reference>); his fears suddenly and strangely vanished, so that he needed to go no further; he <hi type="italic">went his way, and did eat,</hi> and <hi type="italic">his countenance was no more sad,</hi> like Hannah, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.18">1 Sam. i. 18</reference>.  <chapter eID="Ps.77"/> <div eID="gen11879" type="x-p"/>

entries.95dadce959e1a15873e55300eab28b3360e794fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6361"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 77</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.1-Ps.77.20">Psa 77:1-20</reference>. To Jeduthun--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Psa 39:1</reference>, title). In a time of great affliction, when ready to despair, the Psalmist derives relief from calling to mind God's former and wonderful works of delivering power and grace.</title> <div sID="gen9747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6361"/>1. expresses the purport of the Psalm. <div eID="gen9747" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ce9d1641467fab5c1cc893e2964f0c045e17ca2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6362"/><div sID="gen9748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6362"/>2. his importunacy.<div eID="gen9748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9749" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my sore ran ... night--</hi>literally, "my hand was spread," or, "stretched out" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.44.20">Psa 44:20</reference>).<div eID="gen9749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9750" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ceased not--</hi>literally, "grew not numb," or, "feeble" (<reference osisRef="Gen.45.26">Ge 45:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.8">Psa 38:8</reference>).<div eID="gen9750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9751" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my soul ... comforted--</hi>(compare <reference osisRef="Gen.37.35">Ge 37:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.15">Jr 31:15</reference>). <div eID="gen9751" type="x-p"/>
entries.48d144c1ae2a8fbfb19bab9c2673903ac4487ac2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6363"/><div sID="gen9752" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6363"/>3-9. His sad state contrasted with former joys.<div eID="gen9752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was troubled--</hi>literally, "violently agitated," or disquieted (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.6">Psa 39:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.41.5">41:5</reference>).<div eID="gen9753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9754" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my spirit was overwhelmed--</hi>or, "fainted" (<reference osisRef="Ps.107.5">Psa 107:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>). <div eID="gen9754" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2ca50cb7f5d2acb4ac8d1351772788643010f55: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6365"/><div sID="gen9756" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6365"/><hi type="bold">10. Omitting the supplied words, we may read, "This is my affliction--</hi>the years of," &c., "years" being taken as parallel to affliction (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.90.15">Psa 90:15</reference>), as of God's ordering. <div eID="gen9756" type="x-p"/>
entries.3fbb00f8f079d4b00408c0da62e393742f6f7ffa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6366"/><div sID="gen9757" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6366"/>11-12. He finds relief in contrasting God's former deliverances. Shall we receive good at His hands, and not evil? Both are orderings of unerring mercy and unfailing love. <div eID="gen9757" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1f20f218c73d4be1b832266643805ca846efd37: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6367"/><div sID="gen9758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6367"/><hi type="bold">13. Thy way ... in the sanctuary--</hi>God's ways of grace and providence (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.3">Psa 22:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.67.2">67:2</reference>), ordered on holy principles, as developed in His worship; or implied in His perfections, if "holiness" be used for "sanctuary," as some prefer translating (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Ex 15:11</reference>). <div eID="gen9758" type="x-p"/>
entries.30a47c5ecd243c0fb4a5a25068b032bf73ee7f79: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6368"/><div sID="gen9759" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6368"/>14-20. Illustrations of God's power in His special interventions for His people (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.1-Exod.14.31">Ex 14:1-31</reference>), and, in the more common, but sublime, control of nature (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.11-Ps.22.14">Psa 22:11-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hab.3.14">Ha 3:14</reference>) which may have attended those miraculous events (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Ex 14:24</reference>). <div eID="gen9759" type="x-p"/>

entries.efa7d6e00837f9f3872e62b6e154a0ffe214571b: <div eID="gen21077" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21078" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21079" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21079" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21078" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21080" type="x-p"/> The psalmist's ardent prayer to God in the tine of distress, <reference osisRef="Psa.77.1-Psa.77.4">Psa 77:1-4</reference>. The means he used to excite his confidence, <reference osisRef="Psa.77.5-Psa.77.12">Psa 77:5-12</reference>. God's wonderful works in behalf of his people, <reference osisRef="Psa.77.13-Psa.77.20">Psa 77:13-20</reference>. <div eID="gen21080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21081" type="x-p"/> The title, "To the chief Musician, (or conqueror), to Jeduthun, A Psalm of Asaph." On this title we may observe that both Asaph and Jeduthun were celebrated singers in the time of David, and no doubt were masters or leaders of bands which long after their times were called by their names. Hence Psalms composed during and after the captivity have these names prefixed to them. But there is reason to believe also, that there was a person of the name of Asaph in the captivity at Babylon. The author must be considered as speaking in the persons of the captive Israelites, It may however be adapted to the case of any individual in spiritual distress through strong temptation, or from a sense of the Divine displeasure in consequence of backsliding. <div eID="gen21081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21082" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21083" type="x-p"/> I cried unto God - The repetition here marks the earnestness of the psalmist's soul; and the word voice shows that the Psalm was not the issue of private meditation, but of deep mental trouble, which forced him to speak his griefs aloud.
entries.c4dc9383e67c33afc42130d095bb6e77fadc0ad8: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21084" type="x-p"/> My sore ran in the night, and ceased not - This is a most unaccountable translation; the literal meaning of ידי נגרה yadi niggerah, which we translate my sore ran, is, my hand was stretched out, i.e., in prayer. He continued during the whole night with his voice and hands lifted up to God, and ceased not, even in the midst of great discouragements.
entries.70d5dddf490c7a801d63e7882f71878ac9dc9452: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21085" type="x-p"/> My spirit was overwhelmed - As the verb is in the hithpaeI conjugation, the word must mean my spirit was overpowered in itself. It purposed to involve itself in this calamity. I felt exquisitely for my poor suffering countrymen. "The generous mind is not confined at home; <div eID="gen21085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21086" type="x-p"/> It spreads itself abroad through all the public, <div eID="gen21086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21087" type="x-p"/> And feels for every member of the land."
entries.54222b5f7bd073a6d0e69fcf0b8eacea4604b0e0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen21087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21088" type="x-p"/> Thou holdest mine eyes waking - Literally, thou keepest the watches of mine eyes - my grief is so great that I cannot sleep. <div eID="gen21088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21089" type="x-p"/> I am so troubled that I cannot speak - This shows an increase of sorrow and anguish. At first he felt his misery, and called aloud. He receives more light, sees and feels his deep wretchedness, and then his words are swallowed by excessive distress. His woes are too big for utterance. "Small troubles are loquacious; the great are dumb." Curae leves loquuntur; ingentes stupent.
entries.5db6359d8c012d1db504aa79198bc7e9317c07f6: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21090" type="x-p"/> I have considered the days of old - חשבתי chishshabti, I have counted up; I have reckoned up the various dispensations of thy mercy in behalf of the distressed, marked down in the history of our fathers.
entries.9608f171e8cf5e11ecb722be1bfe8c4711067a09: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21091" type="x-p"/> I call to remembrance my song in the night - I do not think that נגינתי neginathi means my song. We know that נגינת neginath signifies some stringed musical instrument that was struck with a plectrum, but here it possibly might be applied to the Psalm that was played on it. But it appears to me rather that the psalmist here speaks of the circumstances of composing the short ode contained in the seventh, eighth, and ninth verses; which it is probable he sung to his harp as a kind of dirge, if indeed he had a harp in that distressful captivity. <div eID="gen21091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21092" type="x-p"/> My spirit made diligent search - The verb חפש chaphas signifies such an investigation as a man makes who is obliged to strip himself in order to do it; or, to lift up coverings, to search fold by fold, or in our phrase, to leave no stone unturned. The Vulgate translates: "Et scopebam spiritum meum." As scopebam is no pure Latin word, it may probably be taken from the Greek σκοπεω scopeo, "to look about, to consider attentively." It is however used by no author but St. Jerome; and by him only here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.23">Isa 14:23</reference> : And I will sweep it with the besom of destruction; scopabo eam in scopa terens. Hence we see that he has formed a verb from a noun scope, a sweeping brush or besom; and this sense my old Psalter follows in this place, translating the passage thus: And I sweped my gast: which is thus paraphrased: "And swa I sweped my gaste, (I swept my soul), that is, I purged it of all fylth."
entries.4225e2c75a0b20c45c0b7a97483f7f43756a5559: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21093" type="x-p"/> Will the Lord cast off for ever? - Will there be no end to this captivity? Has he not said, "Turn, ye backsliders; for I am married unto you: I will heal your backsliding, and love you freely." Will he then be favorable no more? Thus the psalmist pleads and reasons with his Maker.
entries.9b56af5177cb67038a80b385d1da938eddf4597e: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21094" type="x-p"/> For evermore? - לדר ודר ledor vador, "to generation and generation." From race to race. Shall no mercy be shown even to the remotest generation of the children of the offenders?
entries.9223855e03eb4675d6cd6754c7652a6195a6d1b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen21094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21095" type="x-p"/> Hath God - in anger shut up his tender mercies? - The tender mercies of God are the source whence all his kindness to the children of men flows. The metaphor here is taken from a spring, the mouth of which is closed, so that its waters can no longer run in the same channel; but, being confined, break out, and take some other course. Wilt thou take thy mercy from the Israelites, and give it to some other people? This he most certainly did. He took it from the Jews, and gave it to the Gentiles.
entries.18c6781768f262c81d3c7c378349d3305bc69c5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen21095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21096" type="x-p"/> And I said, This is my infirmity - The Hebrew is very obscure, and has been differently translated: ואמר חלותי היא שנות ימימן עליון vaomar challothi hi shenoth yemin elyon; "And I said, Is this my weakness? Years the right hand of the Most High." If חלותי challothi comes from חלה chalah, and signifies to pray, as De Dieu has thought, then his translation may be proper: Precari hoc meum est; mutare dextram Altissimi. "To pray, this my business; to change the right hand of the Most High." I can do nothing else than pray; God is the Ruler of events. Mr. N. M. Berlin translates, "Dolere meum hoc est; mutare est dextra Altissimi." To grieve is my portion; to change (my condition) belongs to the right hand of the Most High. Here שנות shenoth, which we translate years, is derived from שנה shanah, to change. This latter appears to me the better translation; the sum of the meaning is, "I am in deep distress; the Most High alone can change my condition." The old Psalter, following the Vulgate, - Et dixi, Nunc coepi: haec mutatio dexterae Excelsi, - translates: And I said, Now I began this chaunchyng of ryght hand of hihegh (highest) Alswa say, God sal noght kast al man kynde fra his sigt with outen ende: for nowe I began to understand the syker; (the truth); that man sal be brogt to endles; and thar fore, now I said, that this chaunchyng fra wreth to mercy, is thrugh Ihu Criste that chaunges me fra ill to gude, fra noy to gladnes. <div eID="gen21096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21097" type="x-p"/> Once more, Coverdale, who is followed by Matthews and Becke, takes the passage by storm: "At last I came to this poynte, that I thought; O why art thou so foolish? The right hande of the Most Hyest can chaunge all."
entries.9f392caafacda2b83c638a6674851e881a63264e: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen21097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21098" type="x-p"/> I will remember the works of the Lord - I endeavor to recollect what thou hast done in behalf of our fathers in past times; in no case hast thou cast them off, when, with humbled hearts, they sought thy mercy.
entries.120a731bed6b0142c96a8257b79d1f2e4b4098e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen21098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21099" type="x-p"/> Thy way - is in the sanctuary - See <reference osisRef="Psa.73.17">Psa 73:17</reference>. I must go to the sanctuary now to get comfort, as I went before to get instruction. What a mercy to have the privilege of drawing near to God in his ordinances! How many doubts have been solved, fears dissipated, hearts comforted, darknesses dispelled, and snares broken, while waiting on God in the means of grace! <div eID="gen21099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21100" type="x-p"/> Some understand the words, Thy way is in holiness - all thy dispensations, words, and works are holy, just and true. And as is thy majesty, so is thy mercy! O, who is so great a God as our God?
entries.55f3ba3675581cc713177a53220e5f76613e0205: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen21100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21101" type="x-p"/> Thou - doest wonders - Every act of God, whether in nature or grace, in creation or providence, is wondrous; surpasses all power but his own; and can be comprehended only by his own wisdom. To the general observer, his strength is most apparent; to the investigator of nature, his wisdom; and to the genuine Christian, his mercy and love.
entries.2dac23b17c3354cc393f95ae59e33a993e64a138: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen21101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21102" type="x-p"/> The son. of Jacob and Joseph - "The sons which Jacob begat and Joseph nourished." says the Chaldee. The Israelites are properly called the sons of Joseph as well as of Jacob, seeing Ephraim and Manasseh, his sons, were taken into the number of the tribes. All the latter part of this Psalm refers to the deliverance of the Israelites from Egypt; and the psalmist uses this as an argument to excite the expectation of the captives. As God delivered our fathers from Egypt, so we may expect him to deliver us from Chaldea. It required his arm to do the former, and that arm is not shortened that it cannot save.
entries.8404047d3a6592c3b02437adf9d994690dc1c8de: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen21102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21103" type="x-p"/> The waters saw thee - What a fine image! He represents God approaching the Red Sea; and the waters, seeing him, took fright, and ran off before him, dividing to the right and left to let him pass. I have not found any thing more majestic than this. <div eID="gen21103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21104" type="x-p"/> The depths also were troubled - Every thing appears here to have life and perception. The waters see the Almighty, do not wait his coming, but in terror flee away! The deeps, uncovered, are astonished at the circumstance; and as they cannot fly, they are filled with trouble and dismay. Under the hand of such a poet, inanimate nature springs into life; all thinks, speaks, acts; all is in motion, and the dismay is general.
entries.3670f0ea52ff400d0ad4d7d292f5f379968d4ed9: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen21104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21105" type="x-p"/> The clouds poured out water - It appears from this that there was a violent tempest at the time of the passage of the Red Sea. There was a violent storm of thunder, lightning, and rain. These three things are distinctly marked here. <div eID="gen21105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21106" type="x-p"/> 1. "The skies sent out a sound:" the Thunder. <div eID="gen21106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21107" type="x-p"/> 2. "Thine arrows went abroad:" the Lightning. <div eID="gen21107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21108" type="x-p"/> 3. "The clouds poured out water:" the Rain. In the next verse we have, <div eID="gen21108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21109" type="x-p"/> 4. An Earthquake: "The earth trembled and shook," <reference osisRef="Psa.77.18">Psa 77:18</reference>.
entries.b71606502634fd3f468683ac0410d7aa17fa0cc8: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen21109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21110" type="x-p"/> Thy way is in the sea - Thou didst walk through the sea, thy path was through a multitude of waters. <div eID="gen21110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21111" type="x-p"/> Thy footsteps are not known - It was evident from the effects that God was there: but his track could not be discovered; still he is the Infinite Spirit, without parts, limits, or passions. No object of sense.
entries.5f3364f33b826793d761e57dc7ab7c4c3aebea02: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen21111" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21112" type="x-p"/> Thou leddest thy people like a flock - This may refer to the pillar of cloud and fire. It went before them, and they followed it. So, in the eastern countries, the shepherd does not drape, but leads, his flock. He goes before them to find them pasture, and they regularly follow him. <div eID="gen21112" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21113" type="x-p"/> By the hand of Moses and Aaron - They were God's agents; and acted, in civil and sacred things, just as directed by the Most High.  <chapter eID="Ps.77"/> <div eID="gen21113" type="x-p"/>

entries.e413da78c7b5f1fded804be375872c80f95ca20e: <div eID="gen9775" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Comfort Derived from the History of the Past during Years of Affliction</title> <div sID="gen9776" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">“The earth feared and became still,”</hi> says <reference osisRef="Ps.76.9">Psa 76:9</reference>; <hi type="italic">the earth trembled and shook</hi>, says <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference> : this common thought is the string on which these two Psalms are strung. In a general way it may be said of Psalms 77, that the poet flees from the sorrowful present away into the memory of the years of olden times, and consoles himself more especially with the deliverance out of Egypt, so rich in wonders. As to the rest, however, it remains obscure what kind of national affliction it is which drives him to find his refuge from the God who is now hidden in the God who was formerly manifest. At any rate it is not a purely personal affliction, but, as is shown by the consolation sought in the earlier revelations of power and mercy in connection with the national history, an affliction shared in company with the whole of his people. In the midst of this hymnic retrospect the Psalm suddenly breaks off, so that Olshausen is of opinion that it is mutilated, and Tholuck that the author never completed it. But as Psalms 77 and Ps 81 show, it is the Asaphic manner thus to close with an historical picture without the line of thought recurring to its commencement. Where our Psalm leaves off, Hab. 3 goes on, taking it up from that point like a continuation. For the prophet begins with the prayer to revive that deed of redemption of the Mosaic days of old, and in the midst of wrath to remember mercy; and in expression and figures which are borrowed from our Psalm, he then beholds a fresh deed of redemption by which that of old is eclipsed. Thus much, at least, is therefore very clear, that Psalms 77 is older than Habakkuk. Hitzig certainly calls the psalmist the reader and imitator of Hab. 3; ; and Philippson considers even the mutual relationship to be accidental and confined to a general similarity of certain expressions. We, however, believe that we have proved in our Commentary on <hi type="italic">Habakkuk</hi> (1843), S. 118-125, that the mutual relationship is one that is deeply grounded in the prophetic type of Habakkuk, and that the Psalm is heard to re-echo in Habakkuk, not Habakkuk in the language of the psalmist; just as in general the Asaphic Psalms are full of boldly sketched outlines to be filled in by later prophetic writers.  We also now further put this question: how was it possible for the gloomy complaint of Psalms 77, which is turned back to the history of the past, to mould itself after Hab. 3, that joyous looking forward into a bright and blessed future? Is not the prospect in Hab. 3 rather the result of that retrospect in Psalms 77, the confidence in being heard which is kindled by this Psalm, the realizing as present, in the certainty of being heard, of a new deed of God in which the deliverances in the days of Moses are antitypically revived? <div eID="gen9776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9777" type="x-p"/> More than this, viz., that the Psalm is older than Habakkuk, who entered upon public life in the reign of Josiah, or even as early as in the reign of Manasseh, cannot be maintained. For it cannot be inferred from <reference osisRef="Ps.77.16">Psa 77:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.77.3">Psa 77:3</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Gen.37.35">Gen 37:35</reference>, that one chief matter of pain to the psalmist was the fall of the kingdom of the ten tribes which took place in his time. Nothing more, perhaps, than the division of the kingdom which had already taken place seems to be indicated in these passages. The bringing of the tribes of Joseph prominently forward is, however, peculiar to the Asaphic circle of songs. <div eID="gen9777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9778" type="x-p"/> The task of the precentor is assigned by the inscription to Jeduthun (<hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>: Jeduthun), for ל (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Psa 39:1</reference>) alternates with על (<reference osisRef="Ps.62.1">Psa 62:1</reference>); and the idea that ידותון denotes the whole of the Jeduthunites (“overseer over...”) might be possible, but is without example. <div eID="gen9778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9779" type="x-p"/> The strophe schema of the Psalm is 7. 12. 12. 12. 2. The first three strophes or groups of stichs close with <hi type="italic">Sela</hi>.
entries.e6d5192418e6fc7ce08aa12bc03db4c961f74166: <reference osisRef="Ps.77.1-Ps.77.3">Psa 77:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9780" type="x-p"/> The poet is resolved to pray without intermission, and he prays; fore his soul is comfortless and sorely tempted by the vast distance between the former days and the present times. According to the pointing, והאזין appears to be meant to be imperative after the form הקטיל, which occurs instead of הקטל and הקתילה, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.1">Psa 94:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.8">Isa 43:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.17.18">Jer 17:18</reference>, and the mode of writing הקטיל, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.5">Psa 142:5</reference>, 2Ki 8:6, and frequently; therefore <hi type="italic">et audi = ut audias</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.21.3">2Sa 21:3</reference>). But such an isolated form of address is not to be tolerated; והאזין has been regarded as <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. in the sense of <hi type="italic">ut audiat</hi>, although this modification of האזין into האזין in connection with the appearing of the <hi type="italic">Waw consec</hi>. cannot be supported in any other instance (Ew. §234, e), and Kimchi on this account tries to persuade himself to that which is impossible, viz., that והאזין in respect of sound stands for ויאזין. The preterites in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.3">Psa 77:3</reference> express that which has commenced and which will go on. The poet labours in his present time of affliction to press forward to the Lord, who has withdrawn from him; his hand is diffused, i.e., stretched out (not: poured out, for the radical meaning of נגר, as the Syriac shows, is <hi type="italic">protrahere</hi>), in the night-time without wearying and leaving off; it is fixedly and stedfastly (אמוּנה, as it is expressed in <reference osisRef="Exod.17.12">Exo 17:12</reference>) stretched out towards heaven. His soul is comfortless, and all comfort up to the present rebounds as it were from it (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.37.35">Gen 37:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.15">Jer 31:15</reference>). If he remembers God, who was once near to him, then he is compelled to groan (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.55.18">Psa 55:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.3">Psa 55:3</reference>; and on the cohortative form of a <hi type="italic">Lamed He</hi> verb, cf. Ges. §75, 6), because He has hidden Himself from him; if he muses, in order to find Him again, then his spirit veils itself, i.e., it sinks into night and feebleness (התעטּף as in <reference osisRef="Ps.107.5">Psa 107:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>). Each of the two members of <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference> are protasis and apodosis; concerning this emotional kind of structure of a sentence, vid., Ewald, §357, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.
entries.8bb19de19651a26bc3446308b256b7cdd561995e: <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4-Ps.77.9">Psa 77:4-9</reference> <div eID="gen9780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9781" type="x-p"/> He calls his eyelids the “guards of my eyes.” He who holds these so that they remain open when they want to shut together for sleep, is God; for his looking up to Him keeps the poet awake in spite of all overstraining of his powers. Hupfeld and others render thus: “Thou hast held, i.e., caused to last, the night-watches of mine eyes,” - which is affected in thought and expression. The preterites state what has been hitherto and has not yet come to a close. He still endures, as formerly, such thumps and blows within him, as though he lay upon an anvil (פּעם), and his voice fails him. Then silent soliloquy takes the place of audible prayer; he throws himself back in thought to the days of old (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.5">Psa 143:5</reference>), the years of past periods (<reference osisRef="Isa.51.9">Isa 51:9</reference>), which were so rich in the proofs of the power and loving-kindness of the God who was then manifest, but is now hidden. He remembers the happier past of his people and his own, inasmuch as he now in the night purposely calls back to himself in his mind the time when joyful thankfulness impelled him to the song of praise accompanied by the music of the harp (בּלּילה belongs according to the accents to the verb, not to נגינתי, although that construction certainly is strongly commended by parallel passages like <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Psa 16:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.42.9">Psa 42:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.92.3">Psa 92:3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference>), in place of which, crying and sighing and gloomy silence have now entered. He gives himself up to musing “with his heart,” i.e., in the retirement of his inmost nature, inasmuch as he allows his thoughts incessantly to hover to and fro between the present and the former days, and in consequence of this (<hi type="italic">fut. consec</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Ps.42.6">Psa 42:6</reference>) his spirit betakes itself to scrupulizing (what the lxx reproduces with σκάλλειν, Aquila with σκαλεύειν) - his conflict of temptation grows fiercer. Now follow the two doubting questions of the tempted one: he asks in different applications, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.8-Ps.77.10">Psa 77:8-10</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.85.6">Psa 85:6</reference>), whether it is then all at an end with God’s loving-kindness and promise, at the same time saying to himself, that this nevertheless is at variance with the unchangeableness of His nature (Mal 3:6) and the inviolability of His covenant. אפס (only occurring as a 3. <hi type="italic">praet</hi>.) alternates with גּמר (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.2">Psa 12:2</reference>). חנּות is an infinitive construct formed after the manner of the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> <hi type="italic">He</hi> verbs, which, however, does also occur as infinitive absolute (שׁמּות, <reference osisRef="Ezek.36.3">Eze 36:3</reference>, cf. on <reference osisRef="Ps.17.3">Psa 17:3</reference>); Gesenius and Olshausen (who doubts this infinitive form, §245, f) explain it, as do Aben-Ezra and Kimchi, as the plural of a substantive חנּה, but in the passage cited from Ezekiel (vid., Hitzig) such a substantival plural is syntactically impossible. קפץ רחמים is to draw together or contract and draw back one’s compassion, so that it does not manifest itself outwardly, just as he who will not give shuts (יקפּץ) his hand (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.7">Deu 15:7</reference>; cf. <hi type="italic">supra</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.10">Psa 17:10</reference>).
entries.8bdda6ec2c7e4672e722f7437f0bcb6bcfc2506c: <reference osisRef="Ps.77.10-Ps.77.15">Psa 77:10-15</reference> <div eID="gen9781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9782" type="x-p"/> With ואמר the poet introduces the self-encouragement with which he has hitherto calmed himself when such questions of temptation were wont to intrude themselves upon him, and with which he still soothes himself. In the rendering of הלּותי (with the tone regularly drawn back before the following monosyllable) even the Targum wavers between מרעוּתי (my affliction) and בּעוּתי (my supplication); and just in the same way, in the rendering of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.11">Psa 77:11</reference></hi>, between אשׁתּניו (have changed) and שׁנין (years). שׁנות cannot possibly signify “change” in an active sense, as Luther renders: “The right hand of the Most High can change everything,” but only a having become different (lxx and the <hi type="italic">Quinta</hi> ἀλλοίωσις, Symmachus ἐπιδευτέρωσις), after which Maurer, Hupfeld, and Hitzig render thus: my affliction is this, that the right hand of the Most High has changed. But after we have read שׁנות in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.6">Psa 77:6</reference> as a poetical plural of שׁנה, a year, we have first of all to see whether it may not have the same signification here. And many possible interpretations present themselves. It can be interpreted: “my supplication is this: years of the right hand of the Most High” (viz., that years like to the former ones may be renewed); but this thought is not suited to the introduction with ואמר. We must either interpret it: my sickness, viz., from the side of God, i.e., the temptation which befalls me from Him, the affliction ordained by Him for me (Aquila ἀῤῥωστία μου), is this (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.10.19">Jer 10:19</reference>); or, since in this case the unambiguous חלותי would have been used instead of the <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>: my being pierced, my wounding, my sorrow is this (Symmachus τρῶσίς μου, <hi type="italic">inf. Kal</hi> from חלל, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.22">Psa 109:22</reference>, after the form חנּות from חנן) - they are years of the right hand of the Most High, i.e., those which God’s mighty hand, under which I have to humble myself (1Pe 5:6), has formed and measured out to me. In connection with this way of taking <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.11">Psa 77:11</reference></hi>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.12">Psa 77:12</reference></hi> is now suitably and easily attached to what has gone before. The poet says to himself that the affliction allotted to him has its time, and will not last for ever. Therein lies a hope which makes the retrospective glance into the happier past a source of consolation to him. In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.12">Psa 77:12</reference></hi> the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> אזכיר is to be retained, for the כי in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.12">Psa 77:12</reference></hi> is thus best explained: “I bring to remembrance, i.e., make known with praise or celebrate (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.7">Isa 63:7</reference>), the deeds of <hi type="italic">Jāh</hi>, for I will remember Thy wondrous doing from days of old.” His sorrow over the distance between the present and the past is now mitigated by the hope that God’s right hand, which now casts down, will also again in His own time raise up. Therefore he will now, as the advance from the indicative to the cohortative (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>) imports, thoroughly console and refresh himself with God’s work of salvation in all its miraculous manifestations from the earliest times. יהּ is the most concise and comprehensive appellation for the God of the history of redemption, who, as Habakkuk prays, will revive His work of redemption in the midst of the years to come, and bring it to a glorious issue. To Him who then was and who will yet come the poet now brings praise and celebration. The way of God is His historical rule, and more especially, as in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.6">Hab 3:6</reference>, הליכות, His redemptive rule. The primary passage <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exo 15:11</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.68.25">Psa 68:25</reference>) shows that בּקּדשׁ is not to be rendered “in the sanctuary” (lxx ἐν τῷ ἁγίῳ), but “in holiness” (Symmachus ἐν ἁγιασμῷ). Holy and glorious in love and in anger. God goes through history, and shows Himself there as the incomparable One, with whose greatness no being, and least of all any one of the beingless gods, can be measured. He is האל, the God, God absolutely and exclusively, a miracle-working (עשׂה פלא, not עשׂה פלא cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.1.11">Gen 1:11</reference>)<note placement="foot">The joining of the second word, accented on the first syllable and closely allied in sense, on to the first, which is accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> (the tone of which, under certain circumstances, retreats to the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>., נסוג אחור) or monosyllabic, by means of the hardening <hi type="italic">Dagesh</hi> (the so-called דחיק), only takes place when that first word ends in  ה- or  ה-, not when it ends in  ה-.)</note> <div eID="gen9782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9783" type="x-p"/> God, and a God who by these very means reveals Himself as the living and supra-mundane God. He has made His omnipotence known among the peoples, viz., as <reference osisRef="Exod.15.16">Exo 15:16</reference> says, by the redemption of His people, the tribes of Jacob and the double tribe of Joseph, out of Egypt, - a deed of His arm, i.e., the work of His own might, by which He has proved Himself to all peoples and to the whole earth to be the Lord of the world and the God of salvation (<reference osisRef="Exod.9.16">Exo 9:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.15.14">Exo 15:14</reference>). בּזרוע, <hi type="italic">brachio</hi> scil. <hi type="italic">extenso</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.6.6">Exo 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference>, and frequently), just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.75.6">Psa 75:6</reference>, בּצוּאר, <hi type="italic">collo</hi> scil. <hi type="italic">erecto</hi>. The music here strikes in; the whole strophe is an overture to the following hymn in celebration of God, the Redeemer out of Egypt.
entries.fe4189fab2f140cca9ff859ce4290fdeedab0929: <reference osisRef="Ps.77.16-Ps.77.19">Psa 77:16-19</reference> <div eID="gen9783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9784" type="x-p"/> When He directed His lance towards the Red Sea, which stood in the way of His redeemed, the waters immediately fell as it were into pangs of travail (יחילוּ, as in <reference osisRef="Hab.3.10">Hab 3:10</reference>, not ויּחילו), also the billows of the deep trembled; for before the omnipotence of God the Redeemer, which creates a new thing in the midst of the old creation, the rules of the ordinary course of nature become unhinged. There now follow in <reference osisRef="Ps.77.18">Psa 77:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference> lines taken from the picture of a thunder-storm. The poet wishes to describe how all the powers of nature became the servants of the majestic revelation of Jahve, when He executed judgment on Egypt and delivered Israel. זרם, <hi type="italic">Poel</hi> of זרם (cognate זרב, זרף, Aethiopic זנם, to rain), signifies intensively: to stream forth in full torrents. Instead of this line, Habakkuk, with a change of the letters of the primary passage, which is usual in Jeremiah more especially, has זרם מים עבר. The rumbling which the שׁחקים<note placement="foot">We have indicated on <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.36.6">Psa 36:6</reference>, that the שׁהקים are so called from their thinness, but passages like <reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference> and the one before us do not favour this idea. One would think that we have more likely to go back to Arab. <hi type="italic">sḥq</hi>, to be distant (whence <hi type="italic">suḥḳ</hi>, distance; <hi type="italic">saḥı̂ḳ</hi>, distant), and that שׁהקים signifies the distances, like שׁמים, the heights, from שׁחק = <hi type="italic">suḥḳ</hi>, in distinction from שׁחק, an atom (Wetzstein). But the Hebrew affords no trace of this verbal stem, whereas שׁחק, Arab. <hi type="italic">sḥq , contundere , comminuere</hi> (Neshwân: to pound to dust, used e.g., of the apothecary’s drugs), is just as much Hebrew as Arabic. And the word is actually associated with this verb by the Arabic mind, inasmuch as Arab. <hi type="italic">saḥâbun saḥqun</hi> <hi type="italic">( nubes tenues , nubila tenuia )</hi> is explained by Arab. <hi type="italic">sḥâb rqı̂q</hi>. Accordingly שׁהקים, according to its primary notion, signifies that which spreads itself out thin and fine over a wide surface, and according to the usage of the language, in contrast with the thick and heavy פני הארץ, the uppermost stratum of the atmosphere, and then the clouds, as also Arab. <hi type="italic">a‛nân</hi>, and the collective <hi type="italic">‛anan</hi> and <hi type="italic">‛anân</hi> (vid., Isaiah, at <reference osisRef="Isa.4.5">Isa 4:5</reference>, note), is not first of all the clouds, but the surface of the sky that is turned to us (Fleischer).</note> cause to sound forth (נתנוּ, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.68.34">Psa 68:34</reference>) is the thunder. The arrows of God (חצציך, in Habakkuk חצּיך) are the lightnings. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. (instead of which Habakkuk has יחלּכוּ) depicts their busy darting hither and thither in the service of the omnipotence that sends them forth. It is open to question whether גּלגּל denotes the roll of the thunder (Aben-Ezra, Maurer, Böttcher): the sound of Thy thunder went rolling forth (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.29.4">Psa 29:4</reference>), - or the whirlwind accompanying the thunder-storm (Hitzig); the usage of the language (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.14">Psa 83:14</reference>, also <reference osisRef="Ezek.10.13">Eze 10:13</reference>, Syriac <hi type="italic">golgolo</hi>) is in favour of the latter. On <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.77.19">Psa 77:19</reference></hi> cf. the echo in Psa 97:4. Amidst such commotions in nature above and below Jahve strode along through the sea, and made a passage for His redeemed. His person and His working were invisible, but the result which attested His active presence was visible. He took His way through the sea, and cut His path (<hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> plural, שׁביליך, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference>) through great waters (or, according to Habakkuk, caused His horses to go through), without the footprints (עקּבות with <hi type="italic">Dag. dirimens</hi>) of Him who passes and passed through being left behind to show it.
entries.b8d375a291cdf78f586a459f61357ed79fdd14fc: <reference osisRef="Ps.77.20">Psa 77:20</reference> <div eID="gen9784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9785" type="x-p"/> If we have divided the strophes correctly, then this is the refrain-like close. Like a flock God led His people by Moses and Aaron (Num 33:1) to the promised goal. At this favourite figure, which is as it were the monogram of the Psalms of Asaph and of his school, the poet stops, losing himself in the old history of redemption, which affords him comfort in abundance, and is to him a prophecy of the future lying behind the afflictive years of the present.  <chapter eID="Ps.77"/> <div eID="gen9785" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 77
Whoever was the penman of this psalm, the Holy Spirit seems, by his mouth, to have dictated a common form of prayer for the Church in her afflictions, that even under the most cruel persecutions the faithful might not fail to address their prayers to heaven. It is not the private grief of some particular individual which is here expressed, but the lamentations and groanings of the chosen people. The faithful celebrate the deliverance which had been once wrought for them, and which was a testimony of God’s everlasting grace, to animate and strengthen themselves to engage in the exercise of prayer with the greater earnestness.
To the chief musician upon Jeduthun. A Psalm of Asaph.
Psalm 77:1-6
1. My voice came to God, and I cried: my voice came to God, and he heard me. 2. I sought the: Lord in the day of my trouble: my hand was stretched out in the night, and remitted not my soul refused to be comforted. 3. I will remember God, and will be troubled: I will meditate, and my spirit will be oppressed [or overwhelmed] with sorrow. Selah. 4. Thou hast held the watches of my eyes: I am troubled, and will not speak. 5. I have recounted the days of old, the years of ancient times. 6. I will call to remembrance my song in the night: I will commune with my heart, and my spirit will search diligently.
 
1. My voice came to God, and I cried. This is not a mere complaint, as some interpreters explain it, denoting the surprise which the people of God felt in finding that he who hitherto had been accustomed to grant their requests shut his ears to them, and was called upon in vain. It appears more probable that the prophet either speaks of the present feeling of his mind, or else calls to remembrance how he had experienced that God was inclined and ready to hear his prayers. There can be no doubt that he describes the greatness of the sorrow with which he was afflicted; and, in nay opinion, he denotes a continued act both by the past and the future tenses of the verbs. In the first place, he declares that he did not foolishly rend the air with his cries, like many who pour forth bitter cries without measure and at random under their sorrows; but that he addressed his speech to God when necessity constrained him to cry. The copula and, which is joined to the verb cried, should be resolved into the adverb of time when, in this way, When I cried my voice came to God At the same time, he also shows, that although he had been constrained often to reiterate his cries, he had not given over persevering in prayer. What is added immediately after is intended for the confirmation of his faith: And he heard me. The copula and, as in many other places, is here put instead of the causal adverb for. The meaning is, that he encouraged himself to cry to God, from the consideration that it was God’s usual manner to show his favor and mercy towards him.
